<explanation>
Below is a step-by-step guide for drawing a detailed system design diagram of Alertmanager, tailored to the file tree and README you provided. Treat this as a monolithic, full-stack alerting service that includes a HTTP/GRPC API, a clustering subsystem, in-memory stores, a CLI, and two web UIs (Elm and React).  

1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   • Alertmanager is a full-stack, stateless (but clustered) alert‐routing and notification service written in Go.  
   • It ingests alerts (typically from Prometheus), applies grouping, silencing, and inhibition rules, and dispatches notifications via various receivers (email, Slack, PagerDuty, webhooks, etc.).  
   • It exposes a REST/OpenAPI v2 API, a web UI (Elm+React), a command‐line client (amtool), and a metrics endpoint.  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   • cmd/alertmanager → the main HTTP server binary  
   • cmd/amtool → the CLI tool  
   • api/… → auto‐generated HTTP handlers and client code for the API v2  
   • cluster/… → gossip-based peer communication and replication  
   • config/… → parsing the YAML routing, inhibition, silences, and receiver configs  
   • store/…, silence/…, dispatch/… → in-memory stores, dispatch logic (grouping & routing), silence engine  
   • notify/… → individual notifier adapters (email, Slack, PagerDuty, webhook, etc.)  
   • template/… → Go template rendering for notification payloads  
   • ui/app (Elm) + ui/react-app (React) → two separate web UIs  
   • asset/ & embed → static asset bundling into the Go binary  
   • test/… & examples/… → acceptance tests and sample configs  

3. Examine the README for additional insights  
   • README describes alert flow, clustering flags, high-availability requirements, and the OpenAPI contract  
   • There is an architecture diagram (doc/arch.svg) showing:  
     – HTTP ingress → API → core services → dispatch → notifiers  
     – Cluster messaging between peers  
     – CLI & web UI calling into the API  

4. Components & interactions  
   Draw these main boxes and interactions:  
   A. Ingress Layer  
     1. HTTP Server (cmd/alertmanager)  
        – Exposes endpoints:  
          • /api/v2 (OpenAPI handlers in api/v2/restapi)  
          • /metrics (Prometheus metrics via api/metrics)  
          • Web UI assets (embedded Elm and React static files)  
     2. CLI Client (amtool)  
        – Calls the same HTTP API (/api/v2/*) over HTTP  
   B. Core Processing  
     1. Config Loader (config/)  
        – Parses YAML into Route Tree, Inhibition Rules, Receivers  
     2. Store  
        – Alerts Store (in‐memory, store/)  
        – Silences Store (in‐memory, silence/)  
     3. Dispatch Engine (dispatch/)  
        – Applies group_by and routes to build AlertGroups  
        – Checks silences & inhibition rules  
     4. Template Renderer (template/)  
        – Renders notification payloads (email HTML, JSON, Slack markdown)  
   C. Notification Layer  
     – Notify Adapters (notify/email, notify/slack, notify/pagerduty, etc.)  
     – Each adapter implements a common interface (notify/notify.go)  
   D. Cluster Subsystem (cluster/)  
     – Gossip protocol over UDP/TCP  
     – Connection pooling, TLS transport, delegate messages  
     – Replicates state (alerts, silences, etc.) across peers  
   E. Web UIs  
     1. Elm-based UI (ui/app) served as static assets  
     2. React-based UI (ui/react-app) also embedded and served  
   F. External Integrations  
     – Prometheus or any alerting client POSTs to /api/v2/alerts  
     – Prometheus scrapes /metrics  
     – External notifiers (email servers, Slack endpoints, PagerDuty API)  

5. Architectural patterns & principles  
   • Layered architecture: Ingress → Core → Dispatch → Notifier  
   • Modular adapters for every notifier in notify/  
   • In-memory state replication via gossip for HA (distributed state)  
   • OpenAPI‐first API generation (api/v2/openapi.yaml + Go-Swagger)  
   • Embedded static assets (asset/ + Promu + go:embed)  
   • Separation of concerns: config parsing, business logic, transport  

6. Tailoring the diagram for a full-stack application  
   • Show clear frontend/backend separation:  
     – Frontend clients: Web browsers (Elm + React) and CLI (amtool)  
     – Backend server: HTTP API + metrics + static asset server  
   • Database interactions: in-memory stores, replicated via clustering; no persistent disk DB  
   • API layers: public REST endpoints (/api/v2/*), metrics endpoint, web root  

7. Diagramming guidelines  
   – Use boxes for each major component (Ingress, Core, Dispatch, Notifier, Cluster)  
   – Draw arrows to show data flow:  
     • Alerts → HTTP Server → Store → Dispatch → Notifier Adapters → External services  
     • CLI/UI → HTTP Server  
     • HTTP Server → Cluster peers (gossip)  
   – Color-code boxes by layer:  
     • Blue: Ingress (HTTP, CLI, UI)  
     • Green: Core (config, store, dispatch, template)  
     • Orange: Notification adapters  
     • Purple: Cluster subsystem  
   – Label each arrow with protocol or format (HTTP/JSON, gRPC, gossip UDP/TCP, SMTP, Webhook)  
   – Include a legend for colors and shapes  

8. Be very detailed  
   • For each Notify adapter, optionally show one generic “Notifier” box with icons/logos of email, Slack, PagerDuty  
   • Inside “Core”, show sub-modules: Config Parser, Grouping Engine, Silence Engine, Inhibition Engine  
   • For the Cluster box, note “gossip protocol” and “state replication”  
   • Indicate static asset embedding (asset/ and ui/*) flowing into the HTTP server binary  

By following these guidelines, your diagram will faithfully reflect Alertmanager’s layered, modular, clustered architecture and serve as an accurate blueprint for both operational understanding and future extension.
